appraisal_events.evidence: Vaugoubert protests « Oh ! mon Dieu, quelle horreur, s’il avait seulement un soupçon ! Mais je n’ai pas de crainte à cet égard », after which the narrator silently recites « Le Roi jusqu’à ce jour ignore qui je suis, / Et ce secret toujours tient ma langue enchaînée ».
appraisal_events.explanation: Charlus's sardonic thrust (« C’était le moment de lui dire ce que vous désiriez ») and the narrator's Racine tag together expose Vaugoubert's belief in his own secrecy as self-deception, so the ambassador is lowered by the very defence he mounts.

appraisal_events.evidence: « D’Annunzio vous a aperçue d’une loge, il a écrit à la princesse de T… une lettre où il dit qu’il n’a jamais rien vu de si beau. Il donnerait toute sa vie pour dix minutes d’entretien avec vous. »
appraisal_events.explanation: The duchesse is publicly courted with extravagant literary homage and an offer of Ibsen manuscripts, but the narrator's parenthesis about the reporter — « chez qui je n’étais jamais allé » — marks her as a fabulist and puts the whole tribute in an ironic frame.

status_effects.explanation: He comes off worse because his confident denial and his fear of suspicion are staged as transparent to Charlus and to the narrator.
Charlus holds the initiative in the exchange: his verdicts are delivered with authority, his sarcasm lands, and Vaugoubert's panicked reply confirms rather than refutes his reading.
She is stopped, flattered, and solicited as an object of famous men's desire and of exclusive gifts; the local elevation is real though tempered by the reporter's unreliability.

ambiguities: The stance toward the D'Annunzio homage is layered: the narrator discredits the little dark lady on one point only (« chez qui je n’étais jamais allé »), so it is not settled whether the letter and manuscripts are inventions or genuine tributes she is trading on.
